newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair to announce new N.Irish peace proposals.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair to announce new N.Irish peace proposals.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair was due on Wednesday to unveil details of plans to kickstart a stalled Northern Irish peace process which have been cautiously welcomed on both sides of the province's sectarian divide.

But at the same time, Britain turned down a call by Sinn Fein, political arm of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), for talks on Anglo-Irish plans for disarming the guerrillas if they called a new ceasefire.
Blair was to give parliament details of plans worked out with outgoing Irish premier John Bruton to deal with the huge stocks of arms held by guerrillas in the province.
Sinn Fein was guardedly optimistic. Its president, Mitchel McLaughlin, said in a telephone interview with Reuters that Sinn Fein had not seen Blair's statement.
But he said Britain appeared to have largely accepted Sinn Fein's argument "that disarmament discussions should properly and legitimately take place alongside all other issues".

Asked about the possibility of Sinn Fein approaching the IRA for a new ceasefire, McLaughlin replied: "We had four main areas of concern. If Tony Blair addresses them all this afternoon, we will have taken a giant step in that direction."
But McLaughlin strongly hinted Sinn Fein wanted another meeting with British officials.
"If we are to give leadership, we are entitled to know what the British prime minister's thinking is. It is a matter for the British to decide how we are going to get this elucidation," he said.
The British government called off contacts with Sinn Fein last week after the killing of two Northern Irish policemen in an IRA ambush and rejected the call for new talks.
"From Her Majesty's Government's perspective, no further meeting between officials and Sinn Fein is envisaged in the present circumstances," a Northern Ireland Office spokesman said.

David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionists, the main party of the province's Protestant majority who want continued British rule, said after talks with Blair on Tuesday that parallel decommissioning was not his party's "first preference."
But he said: "We indicated that we could go along...provided of course that that is what actually happened."
John Hume, head of the moderate nationalist SDLP, hailed the proposals on Tuesday. "I think a real and historic opportunity now exists to take the gun out of Irish politics for ever."
Hard-line Democratic Unionist Party leader Ian Paisley, however, has accused London and Dublin of having "given in to the IRA" and said his party might quit the all-party talks.
But the government is still optimistic the proposals can open the way to progress in the peace talks.
The key point of the plan is "parallel decommissioning", a proposal made in January 1996 by George Mitchell, the former U.S. senator chairing the year-old peace talks.
The term means the IRA and its rival Protestant guerrillas would give up their arms in stages while talks proceeded.
Blair's predecessor, John Major, rejected this element of Mitchell's proposals and demanded that arms be given up before the guerrillas could enter talks.

In a symbol of the tension in Northern Ireland, police in south Belfast foiled a guerrilla ambush just hours before Blair was to speak after armed men took over a house near a Roman Catholic nationalist area, security forces said.
They recovered two fully loaded AK 47 rifles, a weapon often used by IRA fighters, and arrested one person.

Blair prepared to unveil his proposals in London by meeting a 12-year-old Belfast schoolgirl who wrote him a moving letter asking for peace. Margaret Gibney was invited to Blair's Downing Street office after writing as part of a school project.
Gibney wrote: "In my whole life I have only had one year of peace, so peace is very important to me."

Blair, who wrote back saying he was touched by the letter, spent an hour with Gibney before the two posed for photographers. She told reporters Blair had told her he would do everything he could to get peace in Northern Ireland."
